**[p-115]** In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surat al-Jumu'ah (The Congregation)**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them﴾.

The Shaykh (may God's mercy be upon us and upon him) explained the meaning of "the unlettered" (al-ummiyyin) in *Mudhakkirat al-Dirasa* with his words: "al-ummiyyin, that is, the Arabs. The ummi (unlettered) is one who neither reads nor writes, and so were many of the Arabs." (End of quote.)

It was called ummi in reference to his mother, the day she bore him, as he did not know reading or writing and remained so.

Among what indicates that the intended meaning of "al-ummiyyin" is the Arabs is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent from among them, as His saying indicates: ﴿a messenger from among themselves﴾. The same is indicated by His saying about the Prophet of God, Ibrahim: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your sacred House﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, raise among them a messenger from among themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129].

The Shaykh (may God's mercy be upon us and upon him) said: "This verse is explicit that God answered the supplication of His Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) concerning them." (End of quote.)

In a hadith: "Indeed we are an unlettered nation; we do not write, nor do we calculate." This is a judgment upon the majority, not upon all, because among the Arabs there were those who could write, such as the scribes of the Revelation: Umar, Ali, and others.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a messenger from among themselves﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), as indicated by His saying about the People of the Book: ﴿those who follow the messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

God has made clear that what is written with them is what Jesus (peace be upon him) gave good news of, in His saying: ﴿and a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6].

That he (ﷺ) was unlettered, in the sense of not writing, is shown by His saying: ﴿You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ (p-116) [al-Ankabut: 48].

God also explained the wisdom in his (ﷺ) being unlettered, although he recited His verses to them and purified them, by negating doubt about him. They used to claim that what he (ﷺ) brought was "the fables of the ancients which he had had written down, and which are dictated to him" [al-Furqan: 5]. So He said: ﴿Otherwise, the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ [al-Ankabut: 48].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And others among them who have not yet joined them﴾.

The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on us and on him) said in the aforementioned treatise (al-Mudhakkira): This is conjoined to His saying "among the unlettered" (al-ummiyyin), meaning: the sending of this Prophet (ﷺ) is among the unlettered and among others from them. It has also been said that it is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying "teaches them" (yu'allimuhum), meaning: he teaches them and teaches others from among them. By His saying "and others" is meant every person who comes after the Companions from among the people of Islam until the Day of Resurrection, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾ [al-An'am: 19].

It is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that what is indicated by His saying "and others" is that it "was revealed concerning the Persians, the people of Salman." In any case, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specificity of the occasion of revelation. End of quotation (ā h-).

The earlier discussion of this meaning has already been presented when we spoke on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 10].

However, the Shaykh's words (may Allah have mercy on us and on him) preceded us when we came upon them, for added benefit and comfort.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Ṣ Ḍhālika faḍlu Allāhi yu'tīhi man yashā'u﴾: Ṣ

Allah says: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He bestows it upon whom He wills.﴾

There is disagreement about the referent of the demonstrative "that" (ism al-ishara) here, and about who is meant by those upon whom the bounty was bestowed. Is it the unlettered (ummi) nation, on whom Allah bestowed the sending of a prophet from among them? Or is it the Unlettered Prophet ﷺ, on whom Allah bestowed his being sent as a teacher and guide? Or is it "others" (al-akharun) who did not live to see the time of the Mission but whose call reached them and who recognised its bounty?

Al-Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him and on us) in his study notes (Mudhakkirat al-Dirasa) confined himself to saying: "That," i.e., what was mentioned of the sending of this noble Prophet among the unlettered people, ﴿is the bounty of Allah; He bestows it upon whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾. And of the greatness of this bounty is that He bestowed it upon this nation through this noble Prophet. (End of quotation.)

This statement of his (may Allah have mercy on us and on him) includes the first and second of the three opinions. Allah bestowed a bounty upon the unlettered people by sending this noble Prophet among them, and Allah's bounty upon the Prophet by sending him among them is not, by itself, an indication that there is no disagreement between these three opinions. They are either a variety of difference (ikhtilaf tanawwu') or they are mutually entailing (mutalazimat). Therefore there is no objection to applying all of them together, since the bounty of Allah, exalted is He, encompasses all of them.

The first opinion is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they were before in clear error﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 164]. This is exactly the same as what is in Surah "al-Jumu'ah" (Surah 62), because the bestowing of favour (imtinan) is the same as bounty (tafaḍḍul).

He stated the second opinion in His saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know; and the bounty of Allah upon you has been ever great﴾ [al-Nisa': 113].

He stated the third opinion in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, forceful against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of a critic. That is the bounty of Allah; He bestows it upon whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

His saying "He will bring forth" (fasawfa ya'ti) is equivalent to His saying: ﴿And [He has sent it] to others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 3]. Thus it is a variety of difference (khilaf tanawwu'), and the bounty of Allah encompasses all of them.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 5:

Allah's statement: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books.﴾

The Shaykh—may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him—said in his dictation: This is a parable which Allah struck for the Jews. He likened them to a donkey, and likened the Torah, whose duties they were charged with, to books, that is, comprehensive volumes of beneficial knowledge. He likened their being charged with the Torah to the donkey's carrying those books. Just as the donkey gains no benefit from the beneficial knowledge in the books carried on its back, so too the Jews gained no benefit from the beneficial knowledge in the Torah, because they were charged with following Muhammad (ﷺ) and making his attributes known to the people, but they betrayed, distorted and altered, so what was in their book of knowledge did not benefit them. End of quotation.

The Shaykh—may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him—indicated that the point of resemblance is the non-benefit from what they carried of the Torah, while they knew what it contained of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted has clarified (p-118) this in another place, in His statement: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons, but a party of them surely conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. So they denied the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) while they recognised him as they recognise their own sons, and their knowledge of him did not benefit them.

This verse is among the most severe that one should guard against, especially students of knowledge and its bearers, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5], meaning: their being likened in this parable to this well-known animal.

The Shaykh—may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him—has previously discussed this example in several places of al-Adwa', among them in the second volume at Allah's statement: ﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of a dog﴾ to the end of the verse [al-A'raf: 176].

Among them also in the third volume at Allah's statement: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾ to the end of the verse [Ibrahim: 18].

And among them in the fourth volume at Allah's statement: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people﴾ [al-Kahf: 54], in Surah al-Kahf, with what is sufficient in it.

What should be pointed out is that most exegetes treat this as a simple (mufrad) comparison, and that the point of resemblance in it is single, namely non-benefit from what is carried, like the verse in which it is said:

"Like the she-camels in the desert, which thirst kills, while water is carried upon their backs."

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that it is of the category of the representational (tamthili) comparison, because the point of resemblance is composed of the totality of two things: the carried items being beneficial books, and the carrier being a donkey with no connection to them. This is unlike the verse quoted, since the she-camels could benefit from water if they obtained it, whereas the donkey does not benefit from the books even if they were spread out before its eyes. In this there is an indication that among the causes of the transfer of prophethood away from the Children of Israel entirely is that they reached the point of neglecting the benefit of the trust of conveying and acting upon it, so Allah transferred it to a people more worthy of it and of upholding it.

Surah al-Jumu'ah

Allah's statement: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

Concerning this there is the difficulty, and the answer is like what we mentioned earlier in Allah's statement: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 108].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are allies of Allah to the exclusion of [other] people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said in his dictation: The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and "those who are Jews" are the Jews.

(p-119) The meaning of "hadu" (Jews) is: they returned in repentance to Allah from the worship of the calf.

From the same root is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [Al-A'raf: 156]. Their return from worshipping the calf was by sincere repentance, in that they surrendered themselves to being killed as repentance and turning back to Allah, as He explained it by His saying: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ up to His saying ﴿and He accepted your repentance﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 54].

And His saying: ﴿if you claim that you are allies of Allah to the exclusion of [other] people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said regarding: "if you claim that you are allies of Allah," meaning: if you are truthful in your claim that you are allies of Allah, and sons of Allah and His beloved ones, to the exclusion of others among people, then wish for death, because a true ally of Allah longs to meet Him and to hasten to what He has prepared for him of enduring bliss. End quote.

In his saying, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, there is an indication of the explanation of their claim, which is stated in general terms in the verse, and which Allah explained by His saying about them and the Christians along with them: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 18].

Allah refuted their claim against them by His saying: ﴿Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are mere humans of those He has created.﴾

Similar to this verse is His saying "if you claim" in: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours to the exclusion of [other] people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 94].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said: It has been said that the intended meaning of "wishing" (tamanni) is mubahalah (mutual invocation of a curse), and the purpose of the verse is to make manifest the lie of the Jews in their claim that they are the allies of Allah.

His saying "if you claim" together with His saying "if you are" are two conditions, with the consequent depending on the first, i.e., "then wish for death": if you claim, if you are truthful in your claim. A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the saying of the poet:

"If you seek our help, if you are frightened, you will find from us strongholds of honour adorned by generosity."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 7:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent ahead﴾.

He stated that they will never wish for death, and that the cause is "what their hands have sent ahead." However, [the verse] is meant to clarify what the "what their hands have sent ahead" is, which prevented them from wishing for death.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said in his dictation: "They will not wish for it because of the intensity of their greed for life, as Allah, exalted is He, explained in His saying: ﴿And you will surely find them the most greedy of people for life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96]. So the intensity of their greed for life is because they know that if they die they will enter the Fire; and if they wished for death, they would die on the spot."

As for His saying, ﴿because of what their hands have sent ahead﴾, the "bi" (ba') is causative (sababiyyah), and the effect (musabbab) is the negation of their wishing for it. What their hands have sent ahead is disbelief and sins. End of quotation.

What the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, pointed to regarding the causes, namely their disbelief and their sins, Allah has explicitly clarified in another place in His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich." We will record what they said and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the Burning. That is for what your hands have put forth"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181].

So the "bi" here is also causative, meaning: taste the punishment of the Burning because of what your hands have sent ahead of these mentioned deeds. And because of all of this, they will never wish for death, and one of them would love to be granted a life of a thousand years, but that long life would not remove him from the punishment. They have become certain of destruction and have despaired of the Hereafter.

As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies a people with whom Allah has become angry, who have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 13]. And because of all of this, they did not wish for death, as Allah, exalted is He, has informed us about them. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you."﴾

That is: if you flee from death by not wishing for it, it will not make you escape from it, for it will surely meet you without doubt. "Will meet you" here means "will overtake you" (mudrikukum), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you are, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers built up high﴾ [An-Nisa: 78].

And His saying: ﴿Every soul will taste death﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 9 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you should know.﴾ ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often that you may succeed.﴾

(p-121) This noble verse, and this context, resemble in their meaning and form His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass, that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], together with His saying: ﴿And when you depart from ʿArafat, remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198].

In each of them there is a call, and the call of the pilgrimage is a prayer, a striving, a coming, and a remembrance of Allah; then there is dispersal and departure (ifadah). This links Friday with the pilgrimage in form, though their scale differs, and in manner, though their details vary, and in the topics and rulings there is abundance and variety, both of what is agreed upon and what is disputed, which makes the topics of Friday no less important than the topics of the pilgrimage, and requires attention to them just as attention is given to the pilgrimage.

It has been reported from the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, that he was determined to expand the discussion of these matters as was his custom, may Allah have mercy on him, but his will is effective and his capacity is high. Yet every person senses the extent of the Shaykh's topics, his elaboration, and his verification of issues, so that he refrains and abstains from entering into them out of recognizing his own shortcoming relative to them, especially since linking these topics to the texts of the Qur'an is not a clear matter, as Abu Hayyan indicated in the sense of his words at the end of his tafsir of this surah, after briefly summarizing its rulings. He said, and his text is: "The exegetes have filled many of their pages with rulings and disputes on the matters of Friday which have no connection to the wording of the Qur'an." End of quote.

He indicates that the wording of the Qur'an has no connection to those rulings which the exegetes discussed in the topics of Friday. But the student of the Shaykh's method in al-Adwa', and the one who tastes his style, has not confined himself to the wording alone, that is, the indication of the text by correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqah), and has considered the types of indication: implication (tadammun), necessary entailment (iltizam), allusion (ima'), and alerting (tanbih). He finds that most or all of what the exegetes, the hadith scholars, and the jurists said of these topics are principles derived from those types of indication.

I ask Allah, exalted is He, for right guidance, and I seek His help and success in explaining whatever becomes apparent from that, if Allah wills. If I am successful, it is by a favor from Allah and a service to His Book; otherwise it is an endeavor excused in view of my scholarly shortcoming, and the good of intention. And Allah is the Guide to the straight path.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade.﴾

(p-122) The Shaykh, may Allah exalted have mercy on us and on him, said in his study notes, and his text is: "When the call is made for prayer," i.e., the caller performs it, who is the muezzin, saying: "Hasten to prayer."

And His saying: ﴿on the day of Friday﴾, i.e., from the prayer of the day of Friday, i.e., the Friday prayer. End of quote.

What indicates that the intended meaning is the Friday prayer itself, and not the rest of the prayers of that day, is the presence of "min" (from), which is for partition (tab'id), and then this part is specified by the command, by leaving off trade in His saying: ﴿then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾, because this is specific to Friday rather than others, due to the presence of the khutbah (sermon). It had been specified for them before the revelation of this verse, and they performed it before the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, as will come, Allah willing.

The intended meaning of "nida'" (call) is the adhan, as the Shaykh, may Allah exalted have mercy on us and on him, indicated, and as in His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and play﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 58].

From the Sunnah is his ﷺ saying: "When the prayer time comes, let one of you call the adhan for you."

It has been said: "nida'" linguistically is calling with a raised voice, based on the hadith: "for he has a louder voice than you (andā minka sawtan)."

The Shaykh, may Allah exalted have mercy on us and on him, defined the adhan linguistically at His saying: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot﴾ [al-Hajj: 27], saying: "The adhan linguistically is notification (i'lam)."

From it is His saying: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3], and the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

"Asma' has notified us of her parting, many a sojourner whose stay becomes tiresome."

The adhan is among the distinctive features of this Ummah, a sign of the Muslims and a call to prayer.

The beginning of its legislation:

There is disagreement about when it was first legislated. The correct view is that it began after the Hijrah. Some reports came, but they are weak, that it was legislated on the night of the Isra' or in Makkah.

Among them, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in al-Bazzar: that it was legislated together with the prayer.

(p-123) Among them, from Ibn 'Abbas in Ibn Hibban: that it was legislated in Makkah at the beginning of the prayer.

Ibn Hajar said: none of that is authentic.

As for its legislation after the Hijrah, in Madinah, there are numerous authentic texts clarifying its beginning and its manner.

Among them is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the two Sahihs and others, who said: "When the Muslims came to Madinah, they would gather and watch for the prayer time, and no one called to it. One day they discussed that. Some of them said: 'Take a bell like the bell of the Christians.' Some said: 'A horn like the horn of the Jews.' Then 'Umar said: 'Will you not send a man to call to prayer?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O Bilal, rise and call to prayer.'"

In the Muwatta' of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: "He ﷺ had intended to take two pieces of wood which he would strike, so that the people would gather for prayer. Then 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd al-Ansari was shown two pieces of wood in a dream and he said: 'These two are indeed like what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intends.' He said: 'Will you not call the adhan for the prayer?' So he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he awoke and told him of that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the adhan."

Some other narrations, from other than Ibn 'Umar and outside the two Shaykhs, have other wordings and different forms, among them: they said: "Raise a banner, and when the people see it, one will inform the other," i.e., notify him at the time of the prayer. This did not please him, so the qan' was mentioned to him, which is the shabbur of the Jews, and this did not please him either, and he said: "This is from the affair of the Jews."

In the narration of Anas: "that they should kindle a fire, but nothing of all that pleased him."

In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded that a bell be made, to be struck for the people to gather the prayers, a man came to me in my sleep carrying a bell in his hand. I said: 'O servant of Allah, will you sell the bell?' He said: 'What will you do with it?' I said: 'We call to prayer with it.' He said: 'Shall I not direct you to what is better than that?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Say: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah. Hayya ala al-salah, hayya ala al-salah. Hayya ala al-falah, hayya ala al-falah. Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah.'"

Then he withdrew from me not far, then said: "When you establish the prayer, say: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah. Hayya ala al-salah, hayya ala al-falah. Qad qamat al-salah, qad qamat al-salah. Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah."

When I woke in the morning, I came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him what I had seen. He said: "Indeed it is a true vision, if Allah wills. Stand with Bilal and cast upon him what you have seen, so he may call with it, for he has a louder voice than you." I stood with Bilal and began casting it upon him, and he called with it. He said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard that while he was in his house, and he came out dragging his garment and saying:

"By He who sent you with the truth, O Messenger of Allah, I have seen what he saw." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Then all praise is due to Allah." Narrated by Abu Dawud.

In another narration of his, he said: "I was between sleeping and waking when a comer came to me and showed me the adhan."

From all of this it becomes clear that the correct view regarding the legislation of the adhan is that it was after the Hijrah, in the illuminated city of Madinah.

Here is a question about the legislation of the adhan. Some people said: how is the matter of the adhan left, when it has this importance in the prayer, so that its legislation is a dream seen by some of the Companions? They criticized the chain of the hadith and argued with the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in the two Sahihs and others, where he ﷺ said: "Rise, O Bilal, and call to prayer." The answer to this is from several aspects:

First: the chain of the hadith of 'Abd Allah is authentic, and al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, discussed it, and mentioned its authentication and those who authenticated it. What supports its authenticity is what we presented from the narration of the Muwatta' regarding the intention to take two pieces of wood, then 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd was shown two pieces of wood, and so on. Likewise, the two Sahihs affirm the consultation regarding what would be used to announce the time of prayer.

Second: it does not conflict with the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, because the hadith of Ibn 'Umar did not mention the wording of the call, so the reconciliation between them is either that Bilal was calling with a different formula, then 'Abd Allah saw the adhan and taught it to Bilal.

This aspect may be supported by what came from Abu Layla, who said: "The prayer was conveyed in three stages, and our companions related to us that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'It has pleased me that the prayer of the Muslims be one, to the extent that I was determined to send men into the houses to call the people at the time of prayer, and I was determined to command (p-125) men to stand upon the watchtowers calling the Muslims, until they became breathless or nearly so.'" He said: then a man from the Ansar came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, when I returned to what I saw of your concern, I saw a man as if he wore two green garments; he stood on the mosque and called the adhan, then he sat a sitting, then he stood and said the like of it, except that he said: 'Qad qamat al-salah.' And had it not been that the people would say, I would have said that I was awake, not asleep." He ﷺ said: "Allah has indeed shown you good, so command Bilal, and let him call the adhan." 'Umar said: "As for me, I too had seen the like of what he saw, but since I was forestalled, I felt shy." Narrated by Abu Dawud as well.

In it: he ﷺ had intended to send men into the houses and upon the watchtowers calling to prayer, so Bilal's first call would be of this kind without specified wording. Or Bilal's call in the Sahih, with the wordings of the adhan in the hadith of 'Abd Allah, after he saw what he saw and the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to teach it to Bilal, so he called with it. There is no contradiction in this, as you see.

Third, also: 'Abd Allah's vision of the adhan does not make it legislated merely from his own side, nor dependent upon him, because it came in the authentic saying that a good dream is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood.

This arrangement of the words of the adhan is only from the category [of revelation], so it is far from whisperings and fancies, because in it is the proclamation of the creed and the humbling of Satan, as in the hadith: "Indeed Satan, when he hears the call, turns and flees," etc.

Then, when he ﷺ heard it, he approved it and said: "Indeed it is a true vision," or "Allah has indeed shown you the truth," so it was a Sunnah of approval, just as one approves some people's actions.

Then after that came his ﷺ teaching of Abu Mahdhurah, and it became an established Sunnah. The question would arise had it not reached him ﷺ and they acted upon it merely by the vision; but since it reached him and he approved it, there is no question then.

Fourth: in some narrations it is that revelation had come to him with it, and when 'Umar informed him, he said to him: "Revelation has preceded you in that." Mentioned in the Marasil of Abu Dawud.

It is also mentioned from Ibn al-'Arabi an extended discussion establishing the ruling by vision; the commentator on Badhl al-Majhud mentioned both of these.

(p-126) Among what has been said: the revelation of the adhan's wording and its teaching was delayed until Abdullah [ibn Zayd] saw it and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, related it. This was for two reasons, which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned while announcing it together with the remembrance of Allah. So its coming through the two of them is better, and more honouring to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, than its coming through himself, so that it would not appear to be the concern of someone calling people to praise him. This is a reasonable view, though it is open to question, because if he ﷺ had brought them something greater than that, it would not have been a matter for objection.

From the totality of what has preceded, the basic legislation of the adhan is an established Sunnah. Either he ﷺ had intended to send men to the houses to call them, or he ﷺ approved what Abdullah saw. In that case the origin of the legislation is from him ﷺ, and his approval concerns the wording that Abdullah saw.

* *

The virtue of the adhan and the etiquette of the muezzin

There is no doubt that the adhan is among the best of deeds, and that the muezzin is witnessed on its behalf by everything that hears his voice, whether stone or clay. Etc.

It has come from him ﷺ: "The muezzins will be the longest-necked of people on the Day of Resurrection."

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Were it not for the caliphate, I would have given the adhan."

And he ﷺ said: "The imam is a guarantor, and the muezzin is trusted. O Allah, guide the imams and forgive the muezzins." Related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, along with other virtues of the adhan. It has been said: he is trusted regarding the time. It has also been said: he is trusted regarding the private parts (awrat) of the houses at the time of the adhan. He ﷺ urged the muezzins to perform ablution for it, as in the hadith: "None should call to prayer except one who is in a state of ablution," although a minor ritual impurity (hadath) does not invalidate it by consensus.

Since it stands in this position, there are etiquettes for the muezzins:

Among them: that they should be among the best of people, as in Abu Dawud: "Let your best men give the adhan for you, and let your reciters lead you in prayer." On this basis he ﷺ warned against entrusting the adhan to the wicked (fasiqun), as in the hadith "The imam is a guarantor and the muezzin is trusted," mentioned above. In al-Bazzar there is an addition: "They said: O Messenger of Allah, you have left us competing for the adhan after you. He said: 'There will come after me, or after you, a people whose lowest ones are their muezzins.'"

Among them: singing (taghanni) in it is disliked, because it is remembrance and a summons to the best of acts of worship. It has come from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "I love you for the sake of Allah." Ibn Umar said: "But I hate you for the sake of Allah." He asked: "Why?" He said: "Because you sing in your adhan."

In al-Mughni by Ibn Qudamah: the adhan of a child or of a wicked person is not counted, meaning one who is openly wicked. According to the Malikis: he should not imitate the wicked in his adhan.

(p-127) Among them: that he should not commit a clear error of pronunciation (lahn) in it. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: lahn in the adhan is disliked, since it may change the meaning. For whoever says "ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasula Allah" with a fatha on the lam of rasul, it removes it from being a statement (khabar).

He should not elongate the word akbar, because that would put an alif in it and make it the plural of kibar, which is a drum. He should not drop the ha' from the name of Allah or from as-salat, nor the ha' from al-falah, for what Abu Hurayrah related: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "None among you should call to prayer who merges the ha'." The hadith, which al-Daraqutni related.

As for one who has a speech defect (alsagh) that is not gross, his adhan is permissible. It has been related that Bilal used to say "asmadu" by making the shin a sin (asmadu, i.e., ashhadu with the shin pronounced as sin). Ibn Qudamah transmitted this, but this report has no basis despite its fame on people's tongues, as in Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas.

From this it is necessary to supervise the muezzins regarding these two matters: lahn and talhin (melodious distortion), and likewise wickedness, and the qualities of the muezzins. This is especially so in the lands of the two Holy Sanctuaries, the place of the descent of revelation, the source of emulation, and the destination of those coming from every place to take the etiquettes of the adhan and of muezzins from the people of these blessed lands.

* *

The wordings of the adhan and the iqamah, the preferred ones among them, with explanation of tathwib and tarji'

The basis of the wordings of the adhan and iqamah, in origin, rests on the two hadiths: that of Abdullah ibn Zayd in Medina, and that of Abu Mahdhurah in Mecca after the conquest. Whatever else exists follows them, such as the hadith of Bilal and others, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The hadith of Abdullah is found in the Sunan, meaning in the collections other than al-Bukhari and Muslim, and it is earlier in time, as was mentioned in the discussion of the legislation of the adhan, and that it began in Medina when he ﷺ first arrived there.

The hadith of Abu Mahdhurah is found in the Sunan and in the Sahih of Muslim. al-Bukhari mentioned neither of them, but mentioned the story of the cause of the legislation and the hadith that Bilal was commanded to repeat the adhan in pairs and the iqamah once, as will come, Allah willing.

Accordingly, we shall present the hadith of Abdullah first, because of its precedence in time. Its wordings, as was mentioned at the beginning of (p-128) the legislation, are: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah; Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah; Hayya 'ala as-salah, Hayya 'ala as-salah; Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; La ilaha illa Allah.

Its total is fifteen words, meaning sentences. In it the takbir at its beginning is quadrupled, the rest is doubled, and its last is single.

In it the iqamah is: the takbir at its beginning is doubled in each phrase, and the rest is single except the wording of the iqamah itself. Its wording is: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah; Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah; Hayya 'ala as-salah; Hayya 'ala al-falah; Qad qamat as-salah, qad qamat as-salah; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; La ilaha illa Allah.

Al-Shawkani said: Ahmad and Abu Dawud related it, and al-Tirmidhi said of it: hasan sahih. He mentioned several chains for it, including those in al-Hakim, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban in their two Sahihs, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn Majah.

The hadith of Abu Mahdhurah, and the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah was after the conquest, as in the Sunan, that he "went out with a group of people and met the Prophet ﷺ returning from Hunayn, and his muezzin gave the adhan. Abu Mahdhurah remained with his group imitating it mockingly. He ﷺ heard them and summoned them and said: 'Which of you is the one whose voice I heard raised?' They pointed to Abu Mahdhurah. He detained him and released the others, then said to him: 'Stand and call to prayer,' and he taught him."

As for its wordings: in Muslim's version the takbir at its beginning is doubled. The rest is like the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, with the addition of mention of tarji'. Muslim transmitted it in three places, and with the wording of the takbir only twice:

The first place: "From Abu Mahdhurah himself, that the Prophet ﷺ taught him the adhan: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah; Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah; Hayya 'ala as-salah, Hayya 'ala as-salah; Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; La ilaha illa Allah."

The second place: in the story of the raid, that "he ﷺ used to raid when dawn broke, and he would listen for the adhan. If he heard an adhan he would hold off, otherwise he would raid. He heard a man saying: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Upon the fitrah.' Then the man said: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You have come out of the Fire.'" ... the hadith.

(p-129) The third place: from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the muezzin says: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, and one of you says: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; then he says: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, and he says: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah..." the hadith. All of these are the wordings of Muslim for the adhan of Abu Mahdhurah. Muslim did not mention regarding the iqamah except the hadith of Anas: "He commanded Bilal to repeat the adhan in pairs and the iqamah once." In other than Muslim's collection, the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah came with the takbir at its beginning quadrupled, like the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, and with tarji' and tathwib in Fajr. In these it is stated that tarji' occurs first with a lowered voice.

Then he repeats and raises his voice with the two testimonies. This is in Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i. As for the iqamah, two reports came from Abu Mahdhurah. The first: "The Prophet ﷺ taught me the iqamah twice each: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah; Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah; Hayya 'ala as-salah, Hayya 'ala as-salah; Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah; Qad qamat as-salah, qad qamat as-salah; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; La ilaha illa Allah."

The second: exactly like the adhan, with the takbir quadrupled and without tarji', and the iqamah doubled, i.e.: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah; Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah; Hayya 'ala as-salah, Hayya 'ala as-salah; Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah; Qad qamat as-salah, qad qamat as-salah; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; La ilaha illa Allah.

So the first is like the adhan in Muslim's version, and the second is like the report of the adhan in other collections, without tarji' or tathwib, with the iqamah phrase repeated twice.

This is the total of what came in the basic wordings of the adhan from the two hadiths of Abdullah ibn Zayd and Abu Mahdhurah.

Looking at the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, we find its wordings did not differ, neither in the adhan nor in the iqamah. It has the takbir quadrupled in the adhan, without tathwib or tarji', and the iqamah single except for the phrase of the iqamah itself. As for the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah, it came in several forms for both the adhan and the iqamah.

As for the adhan: in Muslim's version the takbir at its beginning is doubled, and in others it is quadrupled. In all of them there is affirmation of tarji' in the two testimonies, with the first lowered and the second raised, like the rest of the wordings of the adhan. As for the iqamah, it came in pairs, and it came exactly like the adhan in other than Muslim's collection, except for tarji' and tathwib, with the iqamah doubled. So the difference between the two hadiths is as follows:

In the wordings of the adhan there are three points:
First: the mention of tarji'.
Second: tathwib.
Third: the number of takbirs at its beginning.

As for tarji', it must be adopted, because it is later than the conquest, and there is no contradiction in it, since it is an addition of clarification with a sound chain.

As for tathwib, it is established from the hadith of Bilal, and it was also certainly later than the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd. It is established that "Bilal gave the adhan for Fajr, and it was said to him: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is asleep. Bilal cried out at the top of his voice: As-salatu khayrun min an-nawm (Prayer is better than sleep)."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: this phrase was introduced into the call to prayer for the Fajr prayer, meaning that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Make that part of your adhan," so it was restricted to Fajr.

Ibn Qudamah, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in al-Mughni from Bilal: "that the Prophet ﷺ forbade him to make tathwib in the Isha prayer." Ibn Majah related it. And [Ibn Qudamah] said: Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, entered a mosque to pray in it, and he heard a man making tathwib in the adhan for Dhuhr. He went out, and it was asked of him: why? He said: "Innovation has driven me out." Thus by all of this it is required to adopt it only in the Fajr prayer.

As for the takbir at the beginning of the adhan: in Muslim's report from Abu Mahdhurah it is doubled in a phrase, which differs from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, while in other collections it is quadrupled. Looking at the chain of Muslim, it is the sounder chain. Looking at what is in others, you find in it a sound addition, namely the quadrupling of the takbir, so it is obligatory to act upon it, just as it is obligatory to act upon the tathwib and tarji', because the report that agrees with the other hadith is preferable to the one that differs from it.

[p. 131] As for the iqama (the second call immediately before the prayer): in the hadith of Abdullah (ibn Zayd), its wording did not differ, as was mentioned earlier. However, in the hadith of Abu Mahdhura, the iqama has come in several forms, and none of these forms agrees with the hadith of Abdullah. In those forms, the phrases are repeated twice in all of their words, and among them the iqama is like the adhan, with the wording of the iqama repeated twice. The chains (isnad) of all of them are equal.

So do we take the iqama according to the hadith of Abdullah or according to the hadith of Abu Mahdhura? In terms of the science of hadith (sina'a), each of them is equal in its chain.

In the hadith of Abu Mahdhura there is an addition, which is the likening of the iqama to the adhan. If the matter were limited to that, acting on the hadith of Abu Mahdhura for the iqama would be preferable, since it is later and contains a sound addition. However, we find the hadith of Bilal in the Sahih, and also in (Sahih) Muslim, which is that Bilal was ordered to pair (shaf') the adhan and to make the iqama odd (witr). And the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The adhan in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was twice, and the iqama was once once, except that he would say: 'Qad qamati as-salah, qad qamati as-salah' (the prayer has been established, the prayer has been established)." It was narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.

By these two hadiths it is possible to give preference between the hadith of Abdullah and the hadith of Abu Mahdhura regarding both the adhan and the iqama.

From the hadith of Bilal: "We pair the adhan." However, they differ in determining the intended meaning of pairing with regard to the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar"), because pairing applies to two and to four. In the adhan, the takbir is either twice or four times, and both fit the meaning of pairing. But if we consider that every two takbirs are one sentence (jumla), then pairing is achieved by two sentences, making four takbirs. And if we consider each takbir a word (kalima), then pairing is found in one sentence because it includes two words. For this reason the disagreement arose.

However, the phrases of the adhan are not counted by single words but by sentences, because we count our saying "hayya 'ala as-salah" (come to prayer) as one, though in reality it is a sentence comprising several single words. Accordingly, our saying "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar" is one word (kalima), and on this basis the pairing is by repeating it, so there are four takbirs. This agrees completely with the narration of both hadiths and with the hadith of Abdullah.

Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: The hadith of Abu Mahdhura came in the copy of al-Fasi of Muslim with four takbirs. End quote.

By this, all the narrations agree on quadrupling the takbir in the adhan.

[p. 132] As for the iqama, the hadith of Bilal is explicit in making the iqama odd except the phrase "qad qamati as-salah," which is exactly the wording of the iqama in the hadith of Abdullah. The exact text of the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar also says that the iqama is once once except the iqama (i.e., the phrase is repeated twice). On this presentation and this discussion, the preferred view is to act on the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd for both the adhan and the iqama, while taking the tarji' (repetition of the testimonies with a lowered voice) and the tathwib (saying "as-salatu khayrun min an-nawm" in the dawn adhan) from the hadith of Abu Mahdhura for the adhan.

Then we mention what the jurists of the major cities (fuqaha' al-amsar) took from all of this, with a clarification of the result: the permissibility of acting on all of them, God willing.

Ibn Rushd said in al-Bidaya, quoting verbatim: The scholars differed about the adhan in four well-known forms:

The first: the takbir is doubled, the two testimonies (shahadatayn) are quadrupled, and the rest is doubled. This is the view of the people of Madina, Malik and others. The later followers of Malik preferred the tarji' in the two testimonies with a voice lower than the adhan.

The second form: the adhan of the Meccans, and this is what al-Shafi'i said. It is the quadrupling of the first takbir and the two testimonies, and doubling the rest of the adhan.

The third form: the adhan of the Kufans, which is quadrupling the first takbir and doubling the rest of the adhan. This is what Abu Hanifa said.

The fourth form: the adhan of the Basrans, which is quadrupling the first takbir and tripling the two testimonies, "hayya 'ala as-salah" and "hayya 'ala al-falah." It begins with "ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah" until it reaches "hayya 'ala al-falah," then it repeats this a second time, meaning the four phrases in sequence, then repeats them a third time. This is what al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Sirin said.

The reason for the difference among these four groups is the difference in the narrations on this matter, and the difference in the continuity of practice (ittisal al-'amal) among each of them. The people of Madina argue for their view with the practice that continued in Madina, and the Meccans similarly argue with the practice that continued among them. Likewise the Kufans and the Basrans, and each of them has narrations that support its view. End quote.

[p. 133] Then he quoted the texts of each group from the texts we mentioned earlier. He did not cite a text for the view of the Basrans that contains the mentioned tripling, although it was found in the Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq with a good chain, volume 1, page 564, and it was narrated from some of the Companions in the said Musannaf.

He said regarding the iqama: As for its form, according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, the first takbir is doubled, and the rest is single except the phrase "qad qamati as-salah." According to al-Shafi'i it is twice (in that phrase). According to Abu Hanifa, it is in pairs (mathna mathna). As for Ahmad, he gave the choice between single and double in it. End quote.

These are the conclusions of the sayings of the imams of the major cities regarding the wording of the adhan and the iqama. Al-Allama Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, summarized them in Zad al-Ma'ad under the heading: "Chapter on his (ﷺ) muezzins." He said, quoting verbatim:

Abu Mahdhura used to repeat the testimonies in the adhan and double the iqama, while Bilal did not repeat and made the iqama single. Al-Shafi'i and the people of Mecca took the adhan of Abu Mahdhura and the iqama of Bilal, meaning the adhan of Abu Mahdhura according to the narration of quadrupling the takbir. Abu Hanifa and the people of Iraq took the adhan of Bilal and the iqama of Abu Mahdhura. Ahmad, the people of hadith, and the people of Madina took the adhan and iqama of Bilal, that is, quadrupling the takbir without tarji', and single iqama up to the phrase "qad qamati as-salah." He said: Malik differed in two places: repeating the takbir and doubling the phrase of the iqama, for he does not repeat it. End quote.

What he means by Malik differing here is with the people of the major cities. Otherwise he agrees with some of the forms mentioned earlier. As for not repeating the takbir, this follows the hadith of Abu Mahdhura in Muslim, and as for not repeating the phrase of the iqama, this follows some narrations of the hadith of Bilal, namely that the iqama be made odd, in this absolute sense. By this, once again, it becomes clear to you that all those forms are sound, and that they fall under the category of diversity of variety (ikhtilaf al-tanawwu'), and each one followed what is sound and preferred in his view. There is no contradiction at all, except the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Sirin about tripling, which none of the four imams held.

Ibn Taymiyya said a decisive word on this in al-Majmu', vol. 22, p. 66, after mentioning this issue, quoting verbatim: If that is so, then the correct position is the view of the people of hadith and those who agree with them, which is to permit everything that is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this matter, and they do not dislike any of it. The variety in the form of the adhan and iqama is like the variety in the forms of recitation (qira'at), the tashahhud, and the like. No one has the right to dislike what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prescribed for his community. End quote.

[p. 134] Ibn al-Qayyim said in another place in Zad al-Ma'ad, among what should not be disputed, quoting verbatim: This is among the permissible differences, about which no one who does it or leaves it is rebuked.

This is like raising the hands in prayer and not raising them, and like the differences in the kinds of tashahhud, the kinds of adhan and iqama, and the kinds of rites of pilgrimage: ifrad, tamattu', and qiran.

A note (tanbih):
Some reports about tathwib came from 'Umar and some rulers. The correct position is that it is attributed to the Prophet (marfu'), as in the story of Bilal mentioned earlier. It is not far-fetched that what came from 'Umar or others is a repetition of what had previously come from Bilal with the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said regarding it: is it specific to the dawn prayer, or general in every prayer in which the imam is asleep? The correct view is that it is specific to the dawn prayer, and in the adhan, not at the door of the amir or the imam. The report of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar was mentioned earlier regarding one who did tathwib in the adhan of the noon prayer, that he considered it an innovation (bid'a) and left the mosque.

* *

How the adhan is performed:
The adhan is performed slowly and deliberately, because it is a proclamation to those far away, while the iqama is performed quickly (hadran), because it is for those present and near. As for the pronunciation of the adhan, it is pronounced with a final pause (jazm), not with i'rab (inflection).

Al-Mughni says: Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Batta mentioned that during its slow recitation and its gradation, that is, in the adhan and the iqama, one does not connect one part of the speech to another, but pauses firmly. He reported this from Ibn al-Anbari, from the linguists, and said: It was narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "Two things are pronounced with final pause: the adhan and the iqama," and he said: This is an indication of their consensus.

* *

The ruling on the adhan and the iqama:
Ibn Rushd said: The scholars differed about the ruling on the adhan: is it obligatory or a strongly recommended sunna? And if it is obligatory, is it an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) or a collective obligation (fard kifaya)? End quote.

So you see its ruling revolves between the strongly recommended sunna and the individual obligation. The reason for this difference is their differing viewpoints on the purpose of the adhan: is it a right of the time, to announce its entry, or a right of the prayer itself, like one of its remembrances, or is it a mark (shi'ar) of the Muslims that distinguishes them from others?

We will summarize the sayings of the imams, may God have mercy on them, with an indication of the basis of each of them, and then clarify the preferred view, God willing.

First: al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa agreed that it is a sunna, according to what al-Nawawi preferred from al-Shafi'i in al-Majmu', that it is a sunna for everyone, the one praying alone and the congregation, at home and while traveling, meaning that the validity of the prayer does not depend on it.

It is also reported from him that it is a collective obligation, that is, for the congregation or specifically for the Friday prayer. The evidence for them in this is the hadith of the one who prayed badly (hadith al-musi' salatahu), because the Prophet (ﷺ) taught him the ablution and facing the qibla along with it, but did not teach him the adhan or the iqama.

Second: Malik. It is reported from him that he obligated it on mosques where there is congregation, and not on the one praying alone, neither as obligatory nor as sunna.

It is also from him that it is a strongly recommended sunna for mosques of congregation. So Malik distinguished between the one praying alone and the mosques of congregation. In the text of Khalil among them, it is a sunna for a congregation that seeks others for an obligatory timed prayer, even the Friday prayer, meaning that otherwise it is not a sunna. He did not make it for the one praying alone at all. The position from him varied regarding mosques of congregation between obligation and strongly recommended sunna. He used as evidence the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "He would not add to the iqama while traveling except at dawn, and he would say: 'The adhan is only for the imam whom the people gather around.'" Narrated by Malik.

Likewise the report of Ibn Mas'ud and 'Alqama: they prayed without adhan or iqama. Sufyan said: "The iqama of the city was sufficient for them." And Ibn Mas'ud said: "The iqama of the city suffices." Both were narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir with a weak chain (bi-lin).

Third: Among the Hanbalis, al-Khiraqi said it is a sunna, like al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa. Others than al-Khiraqi said like the view of Malik.

Fourth: Among the Zahiris, it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). They use as evidence the hadith of Malik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "When you are on a journey, then call the adhan and establish the iqama, and let the older of you lead you." Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayhi).

They understood the command as obligatory.

This is a summary of the sayings of the imams, may God have mercy on them, with an indication of their evidence in general. Its ruling, as you have seen, revolves between sunna generally according to al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa, and obligation according to the Zahiris.

[p. 136] The strongly recommended sunna or collective obligation according to Malik and others has details.

I have seen the texts for all of them. But among the reasons for disagreement about the ruling on the adhan is the hesitation in consideration: is it a right of the time, to announce the entry of the time, or is it a right of the prayer itself, or is it a mark of the Muslims?

Then, if it is for the time, one call to prayer (adhan) is sufficient, since it accomplishes the announcement and suffices in place of others. Neither someone who has missed the beginning of the time nor someone praying in a mosque where the obligatory prayer has already been performed earlier should call the adhan, nor should one call it for the make-up prayers (qada').

If it is among the rights of the prayer, is it then a condition for its validity, or a independent sunnah?

If it is for the time, for the purpose of announcing it, then this is contradicted by the hadith of the story of their halting (ta'ris) at the end of the night, when only the heat of the sun woke them, and by his ﷺ command to move away from that valley, then their descent and the command to give the adhan and the iqamah. There is then no sense in it being for the time in this hadith, and it is narrated by Malik in al-Muwatta.

If it is for the prayer, then it has two aspects:

The first: when the worshipper is praying alone and does not seek anyone to pray with him.

The second: when they are a congregation.

When he is alone and does not seek anyone to pray with him, then there should be no disagreement that it is not a condition for the validity of the prayer, nor is it obligatory for him, because the adhan is for announcement, and there is no one there whom it is intended to inform.

And there is the hadith of the one who prayed badly, mentioned earlier, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic texts explaining the conditions of the prayer may indicate this. These conditions are: purity, the time, covering the 'awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered), and facing the qiblah.

Regarding purity, the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ (5:6), the verse.

Regarding the time, the Exalted said: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night﴾ (11:114), the verse, and similar to it.

Regarding the 'awrah, the Exalted said: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every mosque﴾ (7:31), the verse.

(p-137) Regarding the qiblah, the Exalted said: ﴿We have seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ (2:144).

As for the adhan, the Exalted said: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and play﴾ (5:58).

And in Surat al-Jumu'ah, regarding this verse, He said: ﴿O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah﴾ (62:9). Both of these are a narration of an occurring event, and there is in them no imperative form like other than the adhan, as mentioned earlier.

As for the hadith of Ibn al-Huwayrith, it concerns a specific group and not a single person, as is the wording of the hadith.

What remains is the consideration of it regarding the congregation: is it obligatory for them or recommended? Since, by the Qur'anic texts mentioned earlier, it is not a condition for the validity of the prayer of an individual, it is therefore not a condition for the validity of the prayer of a congregation either, so the matter is taken as recommended.

Similarly, the hadith of Ibn Abi Sa'sa'a, that Abu Sa'id said to him: "I see you love sheep and the desert. So when you are with your sheep or in your desert and you call the adhan for prayer, raise your voice with the call, for no jinn, nor human, nor anything hears the reach of the muezzin's voice except that it will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection. I heard it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Narrated by al-Bukhari, Malik in al-Muwatta, and al-Nasa'i.

The point of evidence in it is his saying, may Allah be pleased with him: "So when you call the adhan for prayer, raise your voice." From it is understood that if he does not call the adhan, there is nothing upon him, and that it is intended to urge raising the voice for the one who calls the adhan, even if he is in the desert, because of the reward that follows from it.

As for its being a symbol (shi'ar) of the Muslims, it should be that its obligation is tied to the mosques in the settled areas (hadar), so it binds their people, as Malik and al-Shafi'i said regarding the mosques.

Al-Shafi'i said: "They are to be fought over it if they abandon it," mentioned by al-Nawawi in al-Majmu', citing the evidence of raiding at dawn or abandoning it because of hearing it. Similarly, in travel it is tied to the imam, and one should be keen on it (p-138) for his ﷺ practice on all his journeys, in his military expeditions and in his Hajj, as is well known. Beyond that, it is without doubt a sunnah that should not be abandoned.

Ibn Taymiyyah has a division similar to this in al-Majmu', in the twenty-second part: "The adhan has several aspects that follow from this, among them the case of combining two prayers. The sunnah has come with the adhan and iqamah for the first of them, and with suffice with the iqamah for the second, as in combining Zuhr and 'Asr at 'Arafah, and Maghrib and 'Isha' at Muzdalifah according to the correct view. This is among the evidences that it is not obligatory for every prayer."

Among them: there is no adhan for women, meaning it is not obligatory. If they wish the virtue, they may give it quietly. Al-Bayhaqi chapter-headed it, saying: "There is no adhan or iqamah for women," and he cited from Abdullah ibn Umar as a statement (mawquf): "There is no adhan or iqamah for women." Then he cited from Asma', may Allah be pleased with her, as a raised report (marfu'): "There is no adhan or iqamah for women, nor Friday prayer, nor the Friday bath, and she should not lead them, but she should stand in the middle of them." Thus narrated al-Hakam ibn Abd Allah al-Ayli, and he is weak. He said: "It has also been narrated regarding the adhan and iqamah from Anas ibn Malik, both as a statement and as a raised report, and its raised form is weak." This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Sirin and al-Nakha'i.

* *

Multiple muezzins for the Friday prayer and the rest of the five prayers in one mosque

First: regarding Friday, the forms of multiplicity for it in this regard are two: the multiplicity of the adhan, i.e. before the time and after the time; and the multiplicity of muezzins after the time, as will come, Allah willing. As for the multiplicity of the adhan, al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, placed a chapter heading for it in his Sahih under the chapter of Friday, saying: "Chapter: The adhan on the day of Friday," and he cited the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, who said: "The call (nida') on the day of Friday originally, when the imam sat on the pulpit, in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. When Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, became caliph and the people increased, he added a third call at al-Zawra'." So in it is the adhan first for the time, like the rest of the prayers, and in it is an adhan before the time, which Uthman added when the people increased, and this is the third meaning; the other two are the adhan for the time and the iqamah, which existed before.

Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in the commentary a remark, saying: "What contradicts that report is refuted by the fact that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, is the one who added the adhan."

In the tafsir of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ziyadah the narrator, from Burd ibn Sinan, from Makhul, from Mu'adh, that Umar ordered his two muezzins to call the adhan for the people for Friday outside the mosque so that people would hear, and he ordered that it be called before him, as it was in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr. Then Umar said: "We invented it because of the great number of Muslims." End of quote.

Then Ibn Hajar discussed this report and said: it is interrupted (munqati'), then he mentioned that he found something that strengthens it, to the end of his words.

So this is evidence for the multiplicity of the adhan for Friday before the time and at its entry, whether it came from Umar, or from Uthman, or from both of them together, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them both.

As for the place and the time of this adhan: the place has been specified by the text, that it was at al-Zawra'.

Much has been said about identifying al-Zawra', although they agree that it is a place in the market. This accords with the purpose of its legislation, which is to alert the people of the market to the time of Friday for going to it.

As for al-Zawra' itself, the scholars of Madinah's history said: it is the name of the market itself. It was also said: it is a raised place within it, near the Zayt stones, near the grave of Malik ibn Sinan, and near the Aba'a market.

The one fixed thing that has not accepted change is the grave of Malik ibn Sinan, but they say "near it," not "in its place." It has appeared to me that al-Zawra' is the place of the mosque that now exists in the market, opposite the Egyptian gate known as the Mosque of Fatimah. It seems to me that al-Zawra' was distorted into al-Zahra', and al-Zahra' among the people equals Fatimah, due to their frequent saying "Fatimah al-Zahra'." It is certainly known that Fatimah al-Zahra', may Allah be pleased with her, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, had no mosque in this place, so there is no validity to attributing this mosque to her. Nor is there validity to the mosques attributed to Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, in the vicinity of the Musalla mosque now known as the Mosque of the Cloud. The true basis of what is attributed to them, may the pleasure of Allah the Exalted be upon them, is that those places were their standing positions at the Eid prayer ground, and for this reason you find them all in this place where they are located.

The first of them, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, delayed his position behind the position of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he prayed the Eid out of courtesy with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and those after him came, and their places of prayer differed, so those mosques were built in the places where they stood.

(p-140) As for what is attributed to Fatimah al-Zahra', there is no relevance to it and no validity. Some later scholars said: it is attributed to one of the virtuous women of later eras, whose name is Fatimah. Accordingly, perhaps she renewed it and did not found it, because there is also no reason for her to undertake building a mosque so close to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

And in connection with the practice of the judiciary: a deed of conditions of endowment (waqf) for the Ashraf al-Sharaqimah in Madinah al-Munawwarah was presented to me, and in some of the specification of its properties it says: "Located on the road of al-Zawra'," and bounded to the south by the endowment of al-Halabi. The endowment of al-Halabi still exists today, known, situated away from the mosque that presently exists in the south-east, with nothing between it and the said mosque except the wall and the street. The date of this deed is a hundred years before the date of writing these words, i.e., before the year one thousand two hundred of the Hijrah.

With this, it has become clear to me that the place of Uthman's adhan, may Allah be pleased with him, was in that location, and that it was central to the market of Madinah, and its distance from the Prophet's Mosque is estimated at about two hundred and fifty meters approximately.

The first adhan in the time of the Prophet ﷺ was on the minaret, and likewise the adhan for the time in the time of the rightly guided caliphs, and after them. As for this adhan, its beginning was at al-Zawra', then it was moved to the door of the mosque, then it was moved to in front of the imam, and that was in the time of Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, then it was moved to the minaret.

As for its time, I have not found a valid and explicit determination: how long was there between it and the second? And was it after the entry of the time or before it?

Ibn Hajar mentioned in al-Fath a report from al-Tabarani, whose text is: "He ordered the first call to be given at a house of his called al-Zawra', so it was called from it. When he sat on the pulpit, his first muezzin called, and when he descended, he established the prayer." And in another report from him by this route: "He called at al-Zawra' before his going out, so that the people would know that Friday had arrived," until he said: "And it has become clear from what has passed that Uthman introduced it to inform the people of the entry of the prayer time, by analogy with the rest of the prayers, so he joined Friday to them, and kept its particularity of the adhan before the khatib." You see him preferring that it was after the entry of the time and at the time of Uthman's leaving, that is, from his house, and he used to live in that direction. But this does not accord with the purpose of establishing this adhan, because when (p-141) the people increased, he placed it in the market to inform them. If it was after the time, what is its benefit, and how is it counted as third? It would then be a multiplicity of muezzins, not a multiplicity of the adhan.

Furthermore, Uthman's residence, may Allah be pleased with him, was adjacent to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and its location is known until now, and it was known as the Ribat of Uthman. So how could this adhan be made at his leaving, given the distance between al-Zawra' and his place of residence?

Then, it is agreed upon that the adhan before the imam (adhan bayna yadayi al-imam) is the adhan given after the time has entered, and the prayer is valid after it. So the third adhan is like the first for Subh (dawn prayer). In light of this, it is preferred that it was before the time and not after it, like the first for Subh, so that its purpose is achieved. Accordingly, its timing should take into account the interval between it and the second adhan, and what achieves its purpose, which is the return of the people of the market and their preparation for Jumu'ah. This varies with the differences of places and towns. Whether it is before the time or after it, there must be a period between the two in which the people of the market can come to the mosque and catch the khutbah (sermon).

If we take into account what happened to 'Uthman himself during the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he entered the mosque while 'Umar was delivering the khutbah and 'Umar rebuked him for the delay, and then 'Uthman introduced this adhan during his caliphate, we would find the indication that he advanced it before the time, lest anyone else fall into what he himself had fallen into. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The text of Ibn al-Hajj will come, stating that it was before the time.

This is the end of what relates to the multiplicity of the adhan on Friday. The warning about the other calls found on Friday in some regions will come, when discussing what has been newly introduced into the adhan and innovated in it, of what is not part of it, God willing.

* *

As for the multiplicity of muadhdhins (callers) on Friday:

It has come explicitly in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on stoning a pregnant woman for fornication, in a long hadith from Ibn 'Abbas during the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and in it is the text: "'Umar sat on the minbar, and when the muadhdhins had fallen silent, he stood and praised Allah with what is fitting for Him," until the end of the hadith.

This is an explicit text from al-Bukhari that 'Umar had muadhdhins, and they would call the adhan when he sat on the minbar, and he would sit until they finished the adhan, then he would stand and deliver the khutbah. That is, all their adhan was after the time had entered.

(p-142) Ibn al-Hajj said in al-Madkhal: "They were three, calling one after another. Then 'Uthman added another adhan at al-Zawra' before the time." Thus it is established from this that there was a multiplicity of muadhdhins for the Friday prayer, and during the time of 'Umar they were three, calling separately, one after another.

Ibn Hajar also mentioned in Fath al-Bari, within his discussion of the previous hadith, under the heading "The single muadhdhin on Friday," a narration from Ibn Habib that he (ﷺ) "when he ascended the minbar and sat, the muadhdhins called the adhan, and they were three, one after another. When the third finished, he stood and delivered the khutbah."

Then he said: "This is a claim that needs evidence, and it has not come explicitly through a connected chain that would establish the like of it."

Then he said: "Then I found it in Mukhtasar al-Buwayti from al-Shafi'i." And in a ta'liq (annotation) by the Rector of the University in the margin on that, he said, in the Riyadh manuscript of Mukhtasar al-Muzani: "Whether it is in Mukhtasar al-Buwayti or al-Muzani, its attribution to al-Shafi'i is correct, and Ibn Hajar did not comment on the existence of this report with anything."

Al-Nawawi said in al-Majmu': Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Buwayti: "The call (nida') on Friday is the one that takes place while the imam is on the minbar: the muadhdhins begin the adhan all together atop the minaret while the imam sits on the minbar, so that the people may hear, and they come to the mosque. When they finish, the imam delivers the khutbah to them." So this is also the text of al-Shafi'i, which al-Nawawi quotes, on the multiplicity of muadhdhins on Friday atop the minaret all together while the imam is on the minbar. By this, the legitimacy of multiple adhans for Jumu'ah is made manifest, both before and after the time, from the practice of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and from the abundant presence of the approved Companions, may Allah's pleasure be upon them all, which may be described as a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti) among a large number of the Companions, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. Likewise, the legitimacy of multiple adhans after the time is established from the action of the caliphs as well, and the consensus of the Companions upon it, along with a report of disputed authenticity traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for what relates to the adhan for the remaining five prayers, it is as follows:

First: Multiplicity of the adhan. It is established in the hadith of Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum, in his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Bilal calls at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls." Agreed upon. This applies to the Fajr prayer only, because of the multiple indicators in the hadith, among which: "He calls at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls," meaning that the adhan of Bilal before dawn makes food lawful, and the adhan of Ibn Umm Maktum after the time has entered makes food unlawful for the fasting person.

In another narration: "Ibn Umm Maktum would not call until he was told: 'You have become morning, you have become morning.'" And there was a span of time between them, so in some narrations there was nothing between them except that this one descends and that one ascends. Narrated by Muslim.

In a narration by the group (of compilers) from Ibn Mas'ud, he (ﷺ) said: "Let the adhan of Bilal not prevent any of you from his suhur, for he calls, or said: he calls at night, so that your one who is standing in prayer may return, and so that he may wake your sleeper."

Al-Shawkani said: He means the one who stands in night prayer (mutahajjid) to rest, so that he may rise for the Subh prayer energetic, or to take suhur if he has a need for fasting; and to wake the sleeper so that he may prepare for the prayer with ghusl and wudu'. The first indicates their succession with a slight difference, and the other indicates the difference between them. Both are sound in chain.

Al-Nawawi explained this in his commentary on Muslim, and al-Shawkani quoted it from him in Nayl al-Awtar with his words: "The scholars said its meaning is: Bilal would call before dawn, and would wait after his adhan for supplication and the like, then he would watch for dawn. When it drew near, he would descend and inform Ibn Umm Maktum, and Ibn Umm Maktum would prepare himself with purification and other things, then he would ascend and begin the adhan at the first appearance of dawn." This accords with his (ﷺ) saying: "so that your one who is standing may return and wake your sleeper," until its end. It is also confirmed by the report from Ibn Umm Maktum, who was a blind man, so he would not call until he was told: "You have become morning, you have become morning." This first adhan for Fajr is the position of the majority (jumhur) apart from Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, among the four imams. He interpreted Bilal's adhan as a call with other than the words of the adhan.

Al-Shawkani said: Among the Hanafis, it is said that when Bilal called before the time, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to return and say: "Indeed the slave has slept." This report was narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "It is a hadith that is not preserved (ghayr mahfuz)."
