In Fath al-Qadir of the Hanafis, the text is: "The adhan is not called for a prayer before its time has entered, and it is repeated within the time."

Abu Yusuf said: It is permitted for Fajr in the last half of the night. In the commentary it is said: This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, and he said: because of the continuous practice of the people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah). So Abu Yusuf, the companion of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on both of them, agreed with the majority on the legitimacy of the adhan before dawn, before the time. And what Abu Hanifa relied upon is not preserved, and Abu Yusuf permitted it in the last half of the night.

The text of the Malikis is that it is in the last sixth of the night. In Mukhtasar Khalil: "Not preceding the time, except for Subh, which is in the last sixth of the night."

Among the Hanbalis, the meaning is in the following text: Our companions said: "It is permitted to call the adhan for Fajr after midnight, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i," up to his words:

Al-Athram narrated from Jabir, who said: "The muadhdhin of the Mosque of Damascus would call for the Subh prayer in the pre-dawn, by the distance a rider travels six miles, and Makhul did not object to that nor say anything about it." End of quote.

* *

Note (tanbih)

In al-Mughni it is said: "A group of the people of hadith said: If there are two muadhdhins, one of whom calls before the rising of dawn and the other after it, there is no harm, so that the first of them may be distinguished from the second, and they should adhere to that, so that the people may know the difference between the two adhans, as was the case during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)," concluded in summary.

As for the multiplicity of muadhdhins for the remaining five times, it is as follows:

First: The basis for this among the scholars is the hadith of Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum mentioned earlier concerning the Fajr prayer. Then they analogized on the basis of need the remaining prayers, just as they took as evidence for the addition of 'Umar and 'Uthman in Jumu'ah for the sake of greater notification, as has been mentioned.

Second: We set out a summary of the sayings on this among the Shafi'is:

Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim, under the chapter on the recommendation of having two muadhdhins for one mosque, and cited his words on the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had two muadhdhins: Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum."

Then he said the following text: "In the hadith is the recommendation of two muadhdhins for one mosque, one of whom calls before dawn and the other at its appearance."

Our companions said: "If more than two muadhdhins are needed, they appoint three, four, or more according to need."

'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed four because of the need when people were numerous.

Our companions said: "When two or more are arranged for the adhan, it is recommended that they do not call all at once, but rather, if the time allows, they call in sequence. If they dispute over who begins, lots are cast between them. If the time is constricted, then if the mosque is large, they call dispersed in its various parts; if it is small, they stand together and call. This applies when the differing voices do not lead to confusion. If it leads to confusion, only one calls." Concluded.

This is the text of al-Nawawi quoting the view of his companions, i.e., the Shafi'is, on the matter, which he cited in his commentary on Muslim. In al-Majmu' Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, on the wording of the main text, when the author said: "It is recommended that the muadhdhin for the congregation be two," and mentioned the hadith of Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum, "and if more is needed, they should be four, because 'Uthman had four. And it is recommended that one call after another, because that is more effective in notification."

Al-Nawawi said in the commentary: Abu 'Ali al-Tabari said: "An increase to four is permitted." Then he debated the matter with those who opposed him regarding the number. Then he said: "What matters is the public interest (al-maslahah). Just as 'Uthman increased to four for the public interest, it is permitted for others to increase."

It is mentioned from the author of al-Hawi that the number may be up to eight. Then he said: "Branch (far'): " and he cited under it the following text:

"If the mosque has two muadhdhins, one calls after another, as Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum did. If they dispute over who begins, lots are cast between them. If the time is constricted and the mosque is large, they call in its various parts, each in a district, so that the people of that area may hear. If it is small, they call together, provided that this does not lead to confusion."

The author of al-Hawi and others said: "They stop together at it, word by word. If that leads to confusion, one calls." Etc.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, the chapter: "Whoever says: let one muadhdhin call while traveling," and he cited with his chain from Malik ibn al-Huwayrith: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a group of my people, and we stayed with him twenty nights. He was merciful and gentle. When he saw our longing for our families, he said: 'Return and remain among them, teach them, and pray. When the prayer time comes, let one of you call the adhan, and let the oldest of you lead you.'"

Ibn Hajar said in the course of the commentary in Fath al-Bari: "Based on this, there is no implication in his words 'one muadhdhin while traveling,' because even in the settled area only one calls. If there were a need for multiple muadhdhins due to the distance between the parts of a town, each would call in one direction, and they would not all call together."

It has been said: "The first to introduce everyone calling together were the Banu Umayyah."

Al-Shafi'i said in al-Umm: "I prefer that one muadhdhin call after another, and that they not all call together. If the mosque is large, there is no harm in having a muadhdhin in each part of it, making the call audible to those near him at one time." Concluded.

Al-Shinqiti's commentary (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 9 (part 6 of 7):

This which the commentator relayed from al-Shafi'i is present in al-Umm, but with the wording: "There is no harm in having a muezzin for every minaret, so that he may make those near him hear it at one time." End of quote.

This much is sufficient to explain the position of al-Shafi'i and his companions, that plurality (of muezzins) is permissible according to what the public interest requires.

As for Malik, the Muwatta' contains the hadith of Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum as well.

Al-Baji said in his commentary: This hadith indicates the permissibility of appointing two muezzins in a mosque who call to one prayer.

'Ali ibn Ziyad related from Malik: There is no harm in having three or four muezzins call the people to prayer on a journey, in a guard post, or on a ship, and there is no harm in having four or five muezzins appointed in a mosque.

Ibn Habib said: There is no harm, in prayers whose time is wide, such as Subh, Zuhr and 'Isha', for five to ten muezzins to call one after another, and in 'Asr from three to five. In Maghrib, only one muezzin calls.

This is the explicit text of Malik and the Malikis on the permissibility of multiple calls to prayer in one mosque, with them calling one after another.

In the text of Khalil there is the following: "Plurality of them and their sequence, except for Maghrib, and their gathering, each upon one call to prayer."

The commentator al-Kharashi mentioned: from five to ten at Subh, Zuhr and 'Isha', and in 'Asr from three to five, and in Maghrib one or a group. Etc.

Among the Hanbalis, in al-Mughni: a section. It is not recommended to exceed two muezzins, because of the hadith of Bilal and Ibn Umm Maktum as well. Then he said: Except that if need calls for more than these two, then it is permissible.

It is related from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he had four muezzins. If need calls for more than that, it is legislated. When there is more than one muezzin, and one of them makes the people hear, it is strange that they call one after another; because the muezzins of the Prophet (ﷺ) would call one after another. If the announcement is not achieved by one, they call as needed: either each muezzin from a minaret or a side, or all at once in one place.

Ahmad said: If several call from one minaret, there is no harm. If they fear that calling one after another will cause the first time to be missed, they call all together at once.

Among the Hanafis: it is stated in Fath al-Qadir, the commentary on al-Hidayah, in the context of answering the muezzin and repeating the call to prayer, the following text: "If there are more than one muezzin in the mosque, they call one after another, and the precedence is for the first..." until he said: "If it is assumed that they heard it from outside their mosque, the cause is realised in regard to them, so it becomes like their plurality in one mosque. If he hears them together, he answers, considering that his response is to the muezzin of his own mosque."

These are the texts of the Imams, may Allah have mercy on them, on the permissibility of multiple muezzins and multiple calls to prayer in one mosque for one prayer, whether spread out or gathered.

Ibn Hazm said: It is not permissible for two or more to call together at once; if that happens, the one who started is the muezzin... until he said:

It is permissible for a group to call one after another, for Maghrib and other prayers alike, with no difference in all of this. No one from the early generations of this Ummah prohibited the plurality of calls by several muezzins in one mosque.

* *

The wisdom of the call to prayer

As for the wisdom of the call to prayer, the greatest of it is that it is one of the distinctive features of this Ummah, as has already been mentioned regarding the origin of its legislation. It includes the foundations of the creed of Tawhid, proclaimed before the assembly, filling the ears, until it became the emblem of the Muslims.

It is transmitted from the Qadi 'Iyad, may Allah have mercy on him, his saying:

(p-148) Know that the call to prayer is a comprehensive statement of the creed of faith, comprising both the rational and the transmitted matters. Its first part is the affirmation of the Essence and what it deserves of perfections, and its transcendence above their opposites; this is by his saying: "Allahu Akbar", and this expression, with the brevity of its wording, indicates what we have mentioned.

Then it declares the affirmation of Oneness and the negation of its opposite, association, which is impossible with respect to Him, glory be to Him and exalted. This is the pillar of faith and Tawhid, placed before all the duties of the religion. Then it declares the affirmation of prophethood and the testimony to the messengership of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), which is a great principle after the testimony of Oneness, and its place is after Tawhid, because it belongs to the category of permissible acts, whereas those preliminaries belong to the category of obligations. After these foundations come the rational words of the creed. Then it calls to prayer and places it immediately after the affirmation of prophethood, because knowing its obligation comes from the Prophet (ﷺ), not from reason.

Then it calls to success, which is winning and remaining in lasting bliss, and in it is an indication of the matters of the Hereafter, of resurrection and recompense, and these are the last subjects of the creed of Islam. Etc.

By "rational matters" in the creed he means the affirmation of the existence of Allah and that He is one with no partner, which is known among them as the "argument of necessity" (qanun al-ilzam), in which it is said: the existent is either possible of existence or necessary of existence. What is possible of existence is possible of non-existence before it exists, and existence and continuance in non-existence before it exists are equal, so its existence is preferred over its continuance in non-existence, and this preference must have a preferrer, who is Allah, exalted. What is necessary of existence does not need an originator, and it is not permissible for it to be in a state of non-existence; otherwise its originator would need an originator, and the preferrer of its existence over a state of existence would be needed.

Thus the rational necessity requires that there must be an originator who is necessary of existence. This is only in regard to existence alone, and reason has been introduced into some of the attributes that existence entails. The truth is that reason has no role in the creed regarding affirmation or negation, because it is transmitted (sam'iyyah) and is taken only from the Wise Lawgiver, since reason falls short of that. Our purpose is only to draw attention to the inclusion of rational matters here.

We have cited the words of Qadi 'Iyad here in the section on the wisdom of the call to prayer for their cogency, and so that you may know the particularity of the call to prayer in this Ummah and others by it: it is not like the clanging of a hollow bell, nor the sound of a foolish horn, nor the beating of a stupid drum, as is the case with the others. Rather, it is words and a summons that awakens hearts from their slumber, rouses souls from their heedlessness, restrains minds from their preoccupations, and prepares the Muslim for this supreme obligation, the second pillar of Islam and its column.

When he hears "Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar" twice, Allah is magnified in his soul, His majesty is brought to mind, He is sanctified, and everything other than Allah is regarded as small. Nothing distracts him from the remembrance of Allah, because Allah is greater than everything, so nothing should occupy his self away from Him.

When he hears "Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah", he knows that his duty toward Him is obedience to Allah and worship of Him.

When he hears "Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah", he knows that he is bound to respond to the summons of Allah.

When he hears "Hayya 'ala as-salah, hayya 'ala al-falah", he knows that his success lies in his prayer at its time, not in what distracts him from it.

Thus his walking toward it is with humility, and his steps to the mosque are voluntary, with presence of heart and gathering of attention.

From here we also grasp the secret of the listener being asked to imitate the call to prayer after the muezzin, so that he is linked with him in his proclamation, his creed and his feeling, as came in the report of 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, the muezzins have surpassed us," so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Say the like of what they say, and when you finish, ask and you will be given." Related by Abu Dawud.

We have introduced this topic here, although it is not part of the methodology of this book, but for a compelling reason and because of the relevance to the discussion of the call to prayer.

As for the compelling reason: I heard some days ago, while writing in the discussions on the call to prayer, from a radio broadcast of a Muslim Arab country, that a writer objected to the call to prayer especially at Fajr, and at other times through the loudspeaker, saying that it wears on the nerves, especially when people are performing their work or upon finishing and returning to rest, and particularly at dawn when they are asleep. Its impact was painful that this should be issued and broadcast. But one of the preachers of the Friday sermons answered him in a comprehensive sermon, and made him understand that the exhaustion and agitation come only from failing to respond to this call, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) informed that Satan urinates in the ear of the sleeper and ties three knots on him; when he awakens and remembers Allah, one knot is undone, when he performs wudu, another knot is undone, and when he prays, the third knot is undone, and he becomes energetic in the morning, among other sufficient replies.

(p-150) There is no doubt that such writing comes only from someone who does not understand the meaning of the call to prayer.

This is what necessitated presenting the wisdom of the call to prayer, though it departs from the methodology of this book; but given the relevance of the discussions on the call to prayer, this is excused. And success is from Allah.

* *

Imitating the muezzin

Imitating the muezzin is considered a way of linking the listener of the call to prayer and alerting him to its subject. The hadith says: "When you hear the muezzin, say the like of what he says." Related by al-Bukhari.

In another narration by him, "from Mu'awiya, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said, while on the pulpit, like the words of the muezzin up to his saying: 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah.' When the muezzin said 'Hayya 'ala as-salah', Mu'awiya said: 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah,' and likewise for 'Hayya 'ala al-falah'; then he said: 'Thus we heard your Prophet (ﷺ).'"

In al-Nasa'i, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when Bilal stood calling. When he fell silent, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever says the like of this with certainty will enter Paradise.'"

The manner of imitation: in the first hadith, "say the like of what he says," so that one follows him phrase by phrase. In the second hadith, "when he fell silent, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever says the like of this...'" and after the silence the likeness is realised by the coming of the call after the muezzin has finished, so there is ambiguity.

Yet what supports the first is found in Muslim and Abu Dawud: from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the muezzin says 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar,' and one of you says 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar,' then he says 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah,' and he says 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah'; then he says 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah,' and he says 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah'; then he says 'Hayya 'ala as-salah,' and he says 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah'; then he says 'Hayya 'ala al-falah,' and he says 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah'; then he says 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar,' and he says 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar'; then he says 'La ilaha illa Allah,' from his heart, and he enters Paradise."

This is an explicit text that the one imitating the muezzin follows him phrase by phrase to the end, except for the two Hay'alas, for in place of them he says the hawqala. They said: the two Hay'alas are a summons to come toward the one calling, and this applies to the muezzin; but the one imitating the call does not raise his voice and it does not apply to him to call others, so he has no reward for uttering them, and therefore he says "La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah," for two reasons. The first: it is a remembrance for which he is rewarded both privately and publicly. The second: an acknowledgment that he has no power to avoid disobedience nor strength to perform obedience except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty, and in it is seeking help from Allah and His power and strength to answer this call and to perform the prayer in congregation.

The majority have adopted the hadith of 'Umar in Muslim regarding imitating the muezzin throughout the whole call in the manner described above. According to Malik, one suffices with the hawqala, following the hadith of Mu'awiya. The texts of the Maliki books say that this is the well-known position in the school, and the non-well-known position, i.e. the opposite of the well-known, is the requirement to imitate the entire call; this was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari on Khalil.

* *

Some additions to the wording of the call to prayer

The mention of al-hawqalah (saying "there is no power nor strength except with Allah") at al-hay'alah (saying "hasten to prayer, hasten to success") has already been made, in some narrations of Muslim and others. At the testimony of faith, one says additionally: "And I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Muhammad as Messenger, and with Islam as religion." His sins are forgiven.

* *

Invoking blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and asking Allah for al-Wasilah (the Intercessory Station) for him.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As (may Allah be pleased with him): he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "When you hear the muezzin (the one who calls to prayer), say the same as he says. Then invoke blessings upon me, for whoever invokes blessings upon me once, Allah will bless him ten times over. Then ask Allah for al-Wasilah for me, for it is a station in Paradise that is fitting only for one of the servants of Allah, and I hope that I will be he. Whoever asks Allah for al-Wasilah for me, intercession will be made lawful for him."

This applies generally to the adhan (call to prayer) for the five daily prayers, except that some additional supplications have been reported for Maghrib and Fajr.

For Maghrib, al-Nawawi reported that one may say after the call: "O Allah, this is the arrival of Your night and the departure of Your day, and the voices of those who call upon You. Forgive me." And one may supplicate between the adhan and the iqamah (the second call immediately before the prayer). This was mentioned by the author of al-Muhadhdhab, who attributed it to the hadith of Umm Salamah, and al-Nawawi affirmed it in al-Majmu'.

As for hearing the adhan for Fajr, when he reaches "al-salatu khayrun min al-nawm" (prayer is better than sleep), one says: "You have spoken truly and righteously." This was reported by al-Nawawi in al-Majmu'.

And from al-Rafi'i: one says: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke truly. Prayer is better than sleep."

If one hears the muezzin while he is in prayer, the scholars have explicitly stated that he should not repeat it, because in prayer there is (p-152) preoccupation. If he hears it while sitting in the mosque, Ahmad stated explicitly that he should not stand up immediately for the prayer until the muezzin finishes or nearly finishes.

If one enters the mosque while the muezzin is calling the adhan, it is recommended for him to wait until the muezzin finishes and to say what the muezzin says, combining the two virtues. If he does not say the same words but begins the prayer, there is no harm. This was mentioned by the author of al-Mughni from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land⦆ — the verse.

The Shaykh (may the mercy of Allah the Exalted be upon us and upon him) had already drawn attention to the usuli (legal-theoretical) question contained in it, namely the command that follows a prohibition (al-amr ba'da al-hazr). The soundest view on it is that a command which was prohibited is returned to the state it was in before the prohibition was imposed.

Question

The time for going to the Friday prayer. The apparent meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trading⦆ is that the hastening occurs after the call, and that leaving off trade is at that time. Its implication (mafhum) is that before the call there is no obligation to hasten nor to leave off trade. This is evident from the text. However, texts have come urging early attendance (al-bukur) at the Friday prayer, among them His saying ﷺ: "Whoever goes early and arrives early, walks and does not ride, and prays what is within his means..." — the hadith.

And the hadith: "Whoever goes out in the first hour..." to the end of the hadith. Thus early attendance is recommended, and this is accepted. But disagreement has occurred between Malik and the majority (al-Jumhur) regarding the starting point of early attendance, and the meaning of "the first hour": whether it is an hour in the linguistic sense (sa'ah lughawiyyah) or a temporal one, and whether it is the first of the day or the first after the adhan. Malik said: the hour is linguistic, namely the first after the adhan, since hastening is obligatory only after it, and before it there is no obligation.

The majority took the hour to be a temporal hour, and that the first is the first of the day. The view of the majority is the preponderant one, for several reasons:

First: in the wording of the hadith on early attendance, since the word bukur (early attendance) applies only to the first part of the day, and one does not say bukur for what comes after midday; rather it is called 'ashiyy (afternoon), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿morning and evening⦆ [Maryam: 11]. The repetition of bakkara and ibtakara indicates that it is in the early morning and its beginnings. Likewise the expression "whoever goes out" (man rāḥa), since going out (ar-rawāḥ) is at the beginning of the day.

Second: in the hadith, "and prays what is within his means" is a decisive proof that there is a time that allows prayer to the extent of what is within his means. But according to Malik's school there is no room for prayer after the call, especially since in his time ﷺ there was only one adhan, and after the call there is no room for prayer.

Third: what has come from some of the early generations (al-salaf), as previously mentioned, that they would pray four, eight and twelve rak'ahs. All of this cannot occur with the linguistic hours. And what came in al-Naysaburi's tafsir, in his saying: "The roads in the days of the salaf, at the time of the pre-dawn and after dawn, were full of those going early to the Friday prayer, walking with lamps."

It has been said: the first innovation introduced into Islam was the abandonment of early attendance at the Friday prayer. What reflection on this question requires is that the time of hastening has two aspects:

An aspect of obligation and requirement: there is no doubt that this is after the call, except for one whose place is far, such that if he waited until the call is made he would not reach it; then hastening to it before the call is obligatory by consensus, since he cannot perform what is obligatory upon him of the Friday prayer except by that.

And what the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. This is an exception from the apparent meaning of the text previously cited.

The second aspect: an aspect of recommendation and preference. This is not restricted to a time, but depends on the circumstances of the person. Whoever is able to go early, and his early going does not cause him to neglect what is more binding upon him, then early attendance is recommended for him. In accordance with how early his going is within the five hours mentioned in the hadith, so is his reward. Two matters support this meaning:

The first: the hadith, "The angels are at the doors of the mosques recording the first, then the first; when the imam arrives they fold the scrolls and sit listening to the remembrance." So the recording of the first, then the first, before the imam's emergence, indicates the virtue of being first before the call, as previously mentioned.

The second matter: we find that for every obligation there is a recommended counterpart. Hastening to the Friday prayer at the call is obligatory, so it has a recommended counterpart, which is hastening before the call. Just as for prayer, fasting and zakat there is an obligatory and a recommended aspect, so too for hastening there is an obligatory and a recommended aspect: its obligatory part is after the call, and its recommended part is before it. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

The ghusl for Friday

In His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah⦆, the hastening to the remembrance of Allah is ordered upon the call. It is known that this is restricted by preceding purity (sabq al-tuhr) by consensus. It has come in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you rise to the prayer, then wash your faces⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 6], so ritual purity by wudu' became a condition for the validity of prayer.

Here, specifically regarding Friday, nothing has been mentioned concerning purity for it, whether by wudu' or ghusl.

Hadiths have come concerning the ghusl of Friday, among them the hadith of Abu Sa'id, in His saying ﷺ: "The ghusl of the day of Friday is obligatory upon every mature person (muhtalim)." And in another wording: "The purity of the day of Friday is obligatory upon every mature person, like the purity from janabah." This is an explicit text on the obligation of ghusl upon everyone who has reached the age of puberty.

Another hadith has come: "Whoever performs wudu' on the day of Friday, then it is good and sufficient, and whoever washes, then ghusl is better." This is an explicit text on the superiority of ghusl over wudu', and consequently the validity of the Friday prayer with wudu', and this is the view of the majority.

It has come in Malik's Muwatta': that 'Uthman entered on the day of Friday while 'Umar was delivering the khutbah, and he rebuked him for his lateness. He informed him that as soon as he heard the call he performed wudu' and came to the mosque. 'Umar said to him: "And the wudu' too!" — and that was in the presence of the Companions. He did not order him to return to perform ghusl. Had it been obligatory, 'Uthman would not have left it of his own accord, nor would 'Umar have approved him leaving it with his wudu'.

The majority said: the first hadith has had its obligation abrogated (nusikha al-wujub) by the hadith of preference (hadith al-mufadalah) mentioned, and they cited two matters as evidence. The first is this story of 'Umar with 'Uthman.

The second is the saying of 'A'ishah — may Allah be pleased with her: "In the beginning they were workers for themselves; they would come to the mosque and their sweat would intensify, so odours would appear from them, and he ﷺ urged them to perform ghusl. When Allah granted them victory and the non-Arabs (al-'uluj) came to them and they were relieved of the burden of labour, they were given leave in this matter." And this is the view of the majority, as we have mentioned.

The Zahiriyyah hold that ghusl is obligatory, but for the day, not for the Friday prayer, because of the text of the hadith: "The ghusl of the day of Friday," and it does not say "the ghusl for the Friday prayer." They cited for their view texts on grooming the hair and nails and on ghusl in a general form every day without restriction, and they restricted ghusl to the specific day of Friday. Accordingly, whoever has not performed ghusl before the prayer, according to them must perform it after it, and it is not a condition for its validity according to them. What appears to be correct is the validity of the view of the majority, for two reasons:

The first: the appropriateness of ghusl on this day is most fitting for this gathering, as 'A'ishah — may Allah be pleased with her — indicated. If we disregard this appropriateness, then the day of Friday and other days would be equal.

The second: the context of the verse indicates, in a subtle way, the non-obligation of ghusl, since it does not mention the kind of purity required for hastening after the adhan. It is known that there must be purity for it, so it is a reference to the second, general verse concerning all prayers: ﴿When you rise to the prayer, then wash your faces⦆ — the verse. So wudu' suffices, and the virtue is attained by ghusl. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 62, verse 11:**

God's words: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush off to it and leave you standing.﴾

The return of the pronoun to trade alone, without mentioning diversion along with it, is a point requiring explanation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: One of the two has been omitted because the mentioned one indicates it. He cited another reading, "انفضوا إليه" (they rushed off to it), so that the pronoun returns to diversion (lahw). This interpretation may be linguistically acceptable, as in the verse of Nabigha Dhubyani:

*"And indeed I saw myself and Nu'm diverting ourselves therein, while time and life had not yet come to ruin by passing."*

Here he mentioned "time" (al-dahr) and "life" (al-'aysh), and returned a single pronoun to them both, relying on one of them to stand in for the other because the meaning is known. This is, as Ibn Malik said: "Omitting what is known is permissible."

The Shaykh (may God have mercy on him) gave parallels to this in other than pronoun return, such as God's words: ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. The garments that protect from heat also protect from cold, so he mentioned only one of them, since it indicates the other. But the context here is different.

The Shaykh also said about this verse, in removing the appearance of inconsistency: It is not hidden that the original referent of the pronoun is the one common to trade and diversion, as indicated by the particle "أو" (or). But the pronoun returned to trade alone, not to diversion, so there is some incompatibility between it and its referent in general. The answer is that trade is more important than diversion and a stronger cause of their dispersing from the Prophet (ﷺ), because they dispersed on account of the caravan, while the diversion was on account of its arrival. Moreover, in the Arabic language it is permissible for the pronoun to return to one of the two mentioned before it. As for coordination by "أو," it is clear, as in God's words: ﴿And whoever commits a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person﴾ [al-Nisa': 112].

As for "و" (and), it is frequent in it, such as:

- God's words: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is a heavy matter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].
- His words: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].
- His words: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34].

End of quotation.

That is, all these examples mention two things, and the pronoun returns to one of them.

Based on the Shaykh's answer (may God's mercy be upon him), it is possible to say that the pronoun returning to one of the two mentioned is either because the two are equal in extension (ma-sadaq, the set of things to which a term applies), or because of an additional meaning in what the pronoun returns to.

From among the equal ones is God's words: ﴿And whoever commits a fault or a sin﴾, because the two are equal in prohibition and disobedience. From among those with an additional meaning is God's words: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾, where "وإنها" (and indeed it) refers to prayer, that is, the prayer, because it is more specific than the general category of patience. The presence of the more specific implies the presence of the more general, but not vice versa. Also, prayer is a means to patience, as in the hadith: "When a matter of distress troubled the Prophet (ﷺ), he turned to prayer."

[p. 187] Likewise God's words: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾, where the pronoun refers to silver, because hoarding silver is more widespread and those who hoard it are more numerous. The image of hoarding is found in it in a broader form, and among many people. So addressing them was more appropriate. From another angle, since silver is of lesser monetary value and gold is greater, returning the pronoun to silver contains an alert from the lesser to the greater. Thus it is as if it were more comprehensive and general, and more frightening for those who hoard gold.

As for the verse here, the orientation the Shaykh (may God's mercy be upon him) gave for the pronoun returning to trade, the context indicates it, namely in God's words after it: ﴿Say: What is with God is better than diversion and than trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11]. He mentioned the two preceding causes of their dispersing from him (ﷺ), then followed it with a concluding statement indicating that trade is the primary one: ﴿And God is the best of providers﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11]. Provision is the fruit of trade. So this is a Qur'anic clarification for the pronoun returning here to trade rather than diversion. And God knows best.

**Note**

Abu Hayyan said, quoting Ibn 'Atiyya: Consider why trade was placed before diversion in the seeing, since it is more important, and was placed after it with the preference, so that the soul first falls upon the clearer.

He means by "in the seeing": (when they see), and by "with the preference": ﴿Say: What is with God is better than diversion and than trade﴾. That is, because diversion is clearer in appearance. What appears to me, and God knows best, is that in the preference he mentioned diversion only as a matter of fact, because diversion has no good in it at all, so it is not a place for comparison. He delayed mentioning trade so that it would be closer to the mention of provision, due to their connection together. If trade had been placed first here too, the mention of diversion would have intervened between it and God's words: ﴿And God is the best of providers﴾, which does not fit with the reality of comparison.

The author said in *Dafʿ Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Inconsistency from the Verses of the Book):

God's words: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush off to it﴾, the verse.

It is not hidden that the original referent of the pronoun is the common element between trade and diversion, as indicated by the word "أو" (or). But this pronoun returns to trade alone, not to diversion, so there is some incompatibility between it and its referent in general.

Moreover, in the Arabic language it is permissible for the pronoun to return to one of the two mentioned before it.

As for coordination by "أو," it is clear, because the pronoun in reality returns to the common element, which is one but not specific, as in God's words: ﴿And whoever commits a fault or a sin and then throws it onto an innocent person﴾, the verse [al-Nisa': 112].

As for "و" (and), it is frequent in it.

Among its examples in the Qur'an is God's words: ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 45].

And God's words: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾, the verse [al-Tawbah: 34].

*"And indeed I saw myself and Nu'm diverting ourselves therein, while time and life had not yet come to ruin by passing."*
